In mathematics, the '''Laplace–Carson transform''', named for [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Pierre Simon Laplace]] and [[John Renshaw Carson]], is an [[integral transform]] closely related to the standard [[Laplace transform]]. It is defined by multiplying the Laplace transform of a function by the [[Complex number|complex]] variable <math>p</math>.<ref name="debnath">{{cite book |last=Debnath |first=Lokenath |last2=Bhatta |first2=Dambaru |title=Integral Transforms and Their Applications |edition=3rd |publisher=CRC Press |year=2015 |page=247 |isbn=978-1-4822-2357-6}}</ref> This modification can simplify the analysis of certain functions, particularly the [[Heaviside step function|unit step function]] and [[Dirac delta function]], whose transforms become simple constants. The transform has applications in [[physics]] and [[engineering]], especially in the study of vibrations and transient phenomena in electrical circuits and mechanical structures.<ref name="fryba"/>

== Relationship to the Laplace transform ==
The Laplace–Carson transform <math>V^\ast(j,p)</math> is directly defined from the one-sided Laplace transform <math>F(s)</math>. If <math>F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{V(j,t)\}(s)</math> is the Laplace transform of <math>V(j,t)</math>, then the Laplace–Carson transform is given by:

:<math>V^\ast(j,p) = p \mathcal{L}\{V(j,t)\}(p) = p \int^{\infty}_0 V(j,t) e^{-pt} \, dt</math>

where the variable <math>p</math> is used in place of the more common <math>s</math> for the frequency domain.<ref name="debnath"/> Due to the multiplication by <math>p</math>, the transform of a derivative, <math>\mathcal{L}\{V'(t)\} = pF(p) - V(0)</math>, takes a different form that some authors found more convenient for operational calculus.<ref name="fryba"/>

== Definition ==
Let <math>V(j,t)</math> be a [[function (mathematics)|function]] and <math>p</math> a [[complex number|complex]] variable. The Laplace–Carson transform is defined as:<ref name="fryba">{{cite book |title=Vibration of solids and structures under moving loads 
|last=Frýba
|first= Ladislav
|lccn=70-151037
|year=1973
}}</ref>

: <math>
V^\ast(j,p) = p\int^{\infty}_0 V(j,t) e^{-pt} \, dt
</math>

The inverse Laplace–Carson transform is:

:<math>
V(j,t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int^{a_0+i\infty}_{a_0-i\infty} e^{tp} \frac{V^\ast(j,p)}{p} \, dp
</math>
where <math>a_0</math> is a real-valued constant chosen so that the integration path lies to the right of all singularities of the integrand.
